clue.text: Down with the exploit — better half's not mine!

parts.note: an exploit is a daring deed or feat
what belongs to a wife (a man's better half) rather than to me is hers

explanation.surface: A boastful husband dismisses his wife's achievement as nothing to do with him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like a gesture of dismissal, but it is the soft plumage of birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Down is the fine soft plumage of birds, so it is a synonym for the soft covering they grow.

clue.text: Scarce gifted, I twitch body, leg or arm

indicators.note: scarce here suggests letters scattered and sparsely placed, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A not very talented speaker confesses to nervous twitching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scarce' loosely signals that GIFTED is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To be restless and keep shifting one's limbs is to make small nervous movements.

clue.text: Both tall and pure, both can't begin to charm

indicators.note: can't begin says each of the two words loses its opening letter

explanation.surface: A tall, pure figure somehow fails to captivate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both can't begin' drops T from tall and P from pure, leaving ALL and URE.
explanation.definitionFit: Attraction or fascination that draws people in; as a verb it means to entice or captivate.

clue.text: Respect a house that hides a head of gnomes

indicators.note: hides says the house holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: a house is a home

indicators.note: head of takes the opening letter of gnomes

explanation.surface: A home with a gnome on show earns admiration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hides' looks like concealment of a whole gnome, but only the letter at its head goes inside, with the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Honour or tribute paid publicly to someone is a form of reverence or esteem.

clue.text: Lecturers cool, so we like tales or tomes

parts.note: a reader is a senior university lecturer in Britain
hip means fashionable, cool

explanation.surface: Trendy academics are fond of stories and books.
explanation.walkthrough: In British universities a Reader ranks just below a professor.
explanation.definitionFit: The body of people who read a book or publication collectively make up its audience.

clue.text: Greek island has a snack, three-way design

parts.note: Samos is an island in the eastern Aegean, belonging to Greece

explanation.surface: A Greek island offers a three-cornered snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three-way design' describes the snack's triangular shape.
explanation.definitionFit: This Indian pastry is a fried snack folded into a triangle, so its design has three sides.

clue.text: Learned from a rebel, topping endless mice?

indicators.note: topping says the earlier pieces sit above the next in this down answer

parts.note: Jack Cade led a rebellion against Henry VI in 1450

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of mice is cut

explanation.surface: A rebel learns a scholarly lesson from an endless plague of mice.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade is the crossword's stock rebel; 'topping' works because this is a down answer, and 'endless' drops the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholarly or erudite, relating to study and education rather than practical matters.

clue.text: Out getting bread mix, deaf to all advice

indicators.note: a mix is a jumble, so the letters are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone stubbornly goes out for bread despite being warned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mix' rearranges OUT and BREAD together.
explanation.definitionFit: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind, so that no counsel or persuasion gets through.

clue.text: Sat I held fast by boy, but I might bite

indicators.note: held fast by says the boy's name grips the other letters inside

parts.note: Alan is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A dog held tight by a boy warns that it may still nip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' in the definition is the dog speaking; 'held fast by' wraps the boy's name around SAT I.
explanation.definitionFit: This breed of German shepherd dog is a guard dog that could well give someone a nip.

clue.text: With hat turned round, girls show they let us choose

indicators.note: turned round tells us the word for the hat is read backwards

parts.note: a lid is slang for a hat
Emma is a girl's name, so girls can be Emmas

explanation.surface: Girls twirling their hats put on a show offering a choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned round' reverses only the word for the hat; 'show' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A quandary forces a choice between alternatives, so such predicaments are what make us pick.

clue.text: Reluctant breeders turn to gloomy snooze

indicators.note: turn to says the whole run of gloomy plus snooze is read backwards

parts.note: gloomy means sad
a snooze is a short sleep, a nap

explanation.surface: Animals unwilling to mate slump into a depressed doze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn to' reverses SADNAP as a whole, giving PAN then DAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Giant bears from China are famously slow to mate in captivity, making them notoriously reluctant to reproduce.

clue.text: Too soon to swallow half of greasy brew

indicators.note: to swallow says one piece takes another inside it

parts.note: too soon means early

indicators.note: half of takes the first three of the six letters of greasy

explanation.surface: It is too early to gulp down a greasy cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to swallow' signals a container and 'half of' picks the first three letters of greasy.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a bergamot-flavoured black tea, a familiar brew in British kitchens.

clue.text: Doctor erects what should be known to few

definitions.text: what should be known to few

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A physician builds something that ought to stay private.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a verb meaning tamper with, shuffling ERECTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something confidential or hidden is by nature something that only a few people are meant to know.

clue.text: Stopped keeping pale, just like a wrong put right?

indicators.note: keeping says the first word holds the second inside it

parts.note: an engine that stopped died
sallow means pale and sickly

explanation.surface: A referee halted play and set an injustice right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' signals a container. A goal scored wrongly is ruled out by the referee, which puts the wrong right.
explanation.definitionFit: When an invalid goal or claim is ruled out by an official, the error is corrected by rejecting it.

clue.text: House plant meant dull respectability

definitions.meaning: a hardy broad-leaved plant common in Victorian parlours
the plant became a symbol of stuffy middle-class respectability, as in Orwell's novel Keep the ___ Flying

explanation.surface: A potted plant stood for stodgy middle-class propriety.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell's novel Keep the Aspidistra Flying made this parlour plant the emblem of drab British suburban respectability.
explanation.definitionFit: This cast-iron plant filled Victorian parlours and so came to symbolise stuffy, conventional middle-class living.

clue.text: Small breakfast nuts for those of brainbox breed

parts.note: a boiled egg is a light breakfast
nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A light breakfast fuels clever people.
explanation.definitionFit: Intellectuals or swots, the sort of clever people dubbed brainboxes.

clue.text: "Peer wants lamb stewed" — words you may skip or read

definitions.text: words you may skip or read

indicators.note: stewed food is cooked down and mixed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lord requests a lamb casserole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stewed' rearranges PEER and LAMB.
explanation.definitionFit: An introductory passage at the start of a text, which readers often pass over.

clue.text: I'm not on fire: the creeping runner said it

parts.note: a switch that is not on is off
to fire a gun is to shoot

explanation.surface: A plant insists it is not burning.
explanation.walkthrough: A runner is a creeping stem sent out by a plant such as a strawberry.
explanation.definitionFit: A side growth from a plant's main stem, such as a runner sprouting new roots.

clue.text: Miss end of week, an office slave like me?

parts.note: Miss is a title for a girl or young woman
Friday is the last working day of the week

explanation.surface: An overworked office assistant longs for Friday, her week's end.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from Man Friday in Robinson Crusoe, a devoted helper.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a female assistant who handles every odd job in an office, a general dogsbody.

clue.text: A college boss who holds me in discredit

indicators.note: who holds says the dean wraps around the other word

parts.note: a dean heads a college or faculty

explanation.surface: A college head is accused of dishonouring the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'who holds' signals a container; 'A' and 'in' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower someone's dignity or standing is to degrade them, bringing them into disrepute.

clue.text: These sandwiches may make you twist in pain

indicators.note: twist means contort, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some sandwiches cause stomach cramps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twist' rearranges IN and PAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian toasted bread rolls with fillings, a popular café snack.

clue.text: New US state suggests a cattle strain

definitions.text: New US state suggests a cattle strain

parts.words: New US state suggests a cattle strain
parts.note: the US state of New ___ shares its name with a Channel Island breed of dairy cow

explanation.surface: A newly formed American state hints at a breed of cows.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop 'New' from the state's name and what remains is a Channel Island breed of cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: A breed of small dairy cattle from a Channel Island, famous for rich creamy milk.

clue.text: A king splits tights, rough when he has his say

definitions.text: rough when he has his say

indicators.note: splits says the tights are broken open with other letters set in the gap

parts.note: hose are stockings or tights
R, from Latin rex, is the usual abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch bursts his tights and speaks gruffly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splits' signals that the tights are opened to take A and the king inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A voice that is rasping or husky, as after shouting, sounds rough whenever its owner speaks.

clue.text: A legal right put down and put away

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid
to put food down is to eat it, so put down here means ate

explanation.surface: A legal claim is overruled and set aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put down' means consumed, past tense of eat; the solver may read it as cancelled.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange or turn someone off is to push them away from you, putting them at a distance.

clue.text: Britain of old: "no bail out" formed its basis

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of no bail are put out of order

explanation.surface: An ancient British legal principle denied bail to prisoners.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient poetic name for the island of Great Britain, used by classical writers.

clue.text: Darlings so small, when seen in porcine places

indicators.note: seen in says the small word appears inside the pig pens

parts.note: pigs are kept in sties
wee is Scottish for very small

explanation.surface: Tiny beloved ones turn up in pigpens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' signals a container; 'wee' is Scots for little.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are affectionate terms of endearment for loved ones, like honey or dear.

clue.text: Outlandish hat he's shown and dress for dame

indicators.note: outlandish means bizarre or strange, so the letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A man shows off a bizarre hat and a dress fit for a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlandish' shuffles the letters of HAT HE'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-fitting, unwaisted dress for a woman takes its name from a scabbard-like covering.

clue.text: I refute hugging a bird called what's-her-name

indicators.note: hugging says one word wraps around another

parts.note: to refute a claim is to deny it
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a bird-loving woman whose name escapes them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hugging' signals that the word for refute wraps around the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's name is who they are; asking what's-her-name is asking for who she is.
